**Systems insight**: Append-only re-sending makes a loop's input grow with the square of the turns it runs, so detection latency is the knob and the budget ceiling is only a backstop: stopping this loop at turn `{python} LoopCost.half_str` instead of `{python} LoopCost.cap_str` already cuts its input `{python} LoopCost.half_ratio_mult_str`. Every undetected loop's charge lands in $\mathbb{E}[C_{\text{attempt}}]$ of @eq-vol3-cost-per-accepted-task and is divided by the acceptance probability, so it inflates the cost of every accepted task. The saving is gross; the detector's own calls, its false alarms on useful work, and the cleanup it triggers come out of it before it counts, and compaction or cache reuse flatten the quadratic term.

:::

### Intervene through guarded admission

A watchdog finding records its supporting observations, candidate and plan versions, rule, and comparison window. The runtime then holds new work under the control rules of @sec-vol3-controlplane-statemachine, without adding a trajectory state, while policy selects one of the three responses in @tbl-vol3-watchdog-escalation-protocol, in no fixed order. @Fig-vol3-semantic-watchdog traces a period-2 recurrence on the repair's candidate to that hold.

| Response                        | What the runtime does                                                                                        | Condition that limits it                                                                                  |
|:--------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Bounded diagnostic continuation | Stage a truthful watchdog observation and admit a limited investigation or revised proposal                  | The new work must pass the admission check                                                                |
| Controlled backtrack            | Restore a compatible private candidate boundary and revise the continuation while retaining failure evidence | Restored files do not undo external effects; unresolved operations and dependencies must be accounted for |
| End model-directed repair       | Stop ordinary admission, enter guarded finalization, and resolve or transfer remaining duties                | Compensation and trusted cleanup still pass the admission check and settle only on evidence               |

: **Watchdog Escalation Protocol**: Runtime guards enforce the selected response; a prompt warning alone does not constrain subsequent behavior or settle outstanding effects. {#tbl-vol3-watchdog-escalation-protocol}

::: {#fig-vol3-semantic-watchdog fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**From Recurrence to Guarded Response**: Four observations of the repair alternate between two versions of the same change with the same test failure, so $D_t = D_{t-2}$ and @eq-vol3-state-recurrence reports period $k = 2$. Equal digests establish equality of the captured projection only, and a deliberate backtrack can produce the same pattern. The finding records the supporting observations, rule, and window; the runtime then withholds new work and its policy selects one of the three responses of @tbl-vol3-watchdog-escalation-protocol, in no fixed order." fig-alt="Two stacked panels. The top panel, captured projection of candidate ws_r18 revisions, shows four observation boxes t minus 3 through t, alternating version A and version B, each with the same failure, connected left to right. Below each is a digest chip: D t minus 3 equals digest a, D t minus 2 equals digest b, D t minus 1 equals digest a, and D t equals digest b; the t minus 2 and t chips are highlighted in red and joined by a dashed red bracket labeled D t equals D t minus 2, recurrence with period k equals 2. A dashed arrow leads down to the lower panel, watchdog finding and escalation protocol, where retained window of the last m digests leads to finding recorded with observations, rule, window, then to admission hold, new work withheld, noted policy selects one, no fixed order. The hold fans out to three boxes: bounded diagnostic continuation, controlled backtrack, and end model-directed repair."}
![](images/svg/semantic-watchdog-oscillation.svg)
:::

A diagnostic observation might say: “The proposed test invocation was withheld. The same candidate content and test failure recur in the retained window; no changed precondition is recorded. Verify a new hypothesis before requesting another test.” It describes observed repetition rather than asserting that the model cannot repair, and it enters a newly assembled context, not an in-flight stream. Its wording may help the next proposal, but the admission gate supplies the bound if the model ignores it.

If intervention arrives during active work, the runtime records a control hold and withdraws eligibility from in-flight output before the continuation reaches a paused boundary. Cancellation is a request, not evidence that a remote job stopped, so admitted operations keep their records under the settlement rule, and any further investigation passes the admission check.

Backtracking uses the checkpoint rules from @sec-vol3-persistence-checkpointing as a new recovery choice recorded alongside the history it follows. Retain why the prior candidate failed, revalidate evidence for the restored candidate, and enforce any banned command at the admission gate rather than through a prompt instruction. If repair stops, the finalization contract takes over.

::: {#chk-12-progress-evidence .callout-checkpoint title="Progress evidence and intervention"}

A watchdog turns fallible progress evidence into an enforced hold. Test both halves.

- [ ] **Useful repetition**: `ws_r18` is unchanged while its admitted test runs. Why might a repeated-state alarm be premature, and what limits the wait?
- [ ] **Metric direction**: A candidate passes more checks but introduces a new compiler error. Why is improvement in one metric not enough to establish a Pareto improvement or task acceptance?
- [ ] **Policy vs. proof**: What can an attempt ceiling guarantee that a state-hash detector cannot? What can a bounded history miss?
- [ ] **Detection-latency estimate**: Using the loop notebook's quadratic term, estimate how the loop's input tokens change if intervention moves from the notebook's turn to twice that turn, before computing it exactly. Which omitted costs and detector errors could reverse the gross saving per accepted task?
- [ ] **Outstanding work**: A watchdog holds new proposals after a test timeout. Which effect and charge obligations remain, and why does the hold not establish that the test stopped?

:::

A progress monitor governs one trajectory. Repeated failures may instead reflect a degraded dependency shared by many trajectories, whose aggregate retries per-trajectory bounds leave uncapped, and the next section moves control to the dependency boundary.

## Tool Circuit Breakers {#sec-vol3-sagas-containment}

The repair's test service becomes slow while several trajectories are waiting on it. A watchdog can hold one trajectory that is not advancing, but others keep submitting tests to the same overloaded dependency, and client libraries add retries beneath their proposals. Recovery therefore needs a limit on aggregate dependency load as well as a limit on each task's work.

A slowdown alone does not imply an increasing request rate. For a fixed population of sequential clients, longer response time actually reduces the rate of new requests. Amplification arises when retries add attempts, a timeout leaves remote work running while a replacement starts, retry layers repeat the same request, or simultaneous failures synchronize the next wave of arrivals.[^fn-metastable-retry-failure] The runtime must identify which mechanism is producing load rather than treat every timeout as a reason for another attempt.

[^fn-metastable-retry-failure]: **Metastable failure**: Retry amplification can outlive its trigger. Bronson and colleagues describe systems in which a brief overload causes failures whose retries keep offered load above capacity after the original cause has gone, so the system stays degraded until load is shed or the retry policy changes [@bronson2021metastable]. A shared tool dependency serving many trajectories is exposed to the same feedback loop. \index{Metastable failure!retry amplification}

Three controls address different parts of the problem. A circuit breaker withholds new calls based on recent dependency evidence, backoff and jitter delay and spread justified retries, and bounded execution and queues limit the resources retained while work waits. None establishes whether the earlier `test_r18` operation finished.

### Scope the breaker and its evidence

A **circuit breaker**\index{Circuit breaker!definition} maintains an admission policy for a defined dependency scope [@nygard2007releaseit]. The scope might be a service operation, region, resource partition, or tenant allocation, and a tenant-specific quota response should disable only that tenant's allocation. The policy defines which failures contribute to the breaker, its observation window and minimum evidence, and the conditions for reconsidering service.

Classification is the central design decision. An outcome counts against the scope when it reflects the dependency's ability to serve, as with a connection failure, a transport timeout, a server error, or a throttling response issued for that scope. An outcome that reflects the request counts as a breaker success even when the task fails, as with a validation rejection of a malformed call, an authorization denial, or a correct domain answer such as “record not found.” Counting those would let one trajectory's bad requests shut off a healthy service for everyone. Over a window $W$ of recent classified outcomes, with $e_i = 1$ for a counted failure and $0$ otherwise, the breaker trips when

$$|W| \ge n_{\min} \quad\text{and}\quad r = \frac{1}{|W|}\sum_{i \in W} e_i \ge r_{\text{trip}},$$ {#eq-vol3-breaker-trip}

where the minimum evidence $n_{\min}$ keeps one failure among a few calls from opening the breaker, and $r_{\text{trip}}$ is the policy's failure-fraction threshold.

@Tbl-vol3-circuit-breaker-states gives the familiar three-state pattern, with meanings restricted to this admission gate. These are breaker states, separate from the trajectory states in @sec-vol3-controlplane-statemachine.

| Breaker state | Admission policy                                                                   | Evidence used to change it                                                             |
|:--------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `CLOSED`      | Permit consideration of calls; the admission check and repeat contract still apply | Current scoped outcomes meet the configured trip rule                                  |
| `OPEN`        | Withhold new ordinary calls to this scope                                          | Cooldown and current policy permit a limited trial                                     |
| `HALF_OPEN`   | Admit only the bounded probe allowance; hold or reject other calls                 | Current-generation probe evidence supports reopening or a controlled return to service |

: **Scoped Circuit-Breaker States**: The breaker controls new admissions through its boundary. It does not cancel already forwarded requests or certify dependency capacity. {#tbl-vol3-circuit-breaker-states}

Opening the breaker governs new calls only. The runtime records a withheld request as not dispatched *through this gate*, and older attempts keep their outcomes under the settlement rule. A structured observation naming the scope and the reason can inform a revised plan, but enforcement comes from the gate, not from assuming the model will obey an error message.

Half-open admission needs coordination. For a single-probe policy, the gateway atomically claims the probe slot before sending, so concurrent callers cannot all become the probe. Each trial cycle gets a `breaker_generation`, recorded with the probe identity at admission, and only a completion matching the current trial may decide its transition. This counter is local breaker metadata, distinct from trajectory `control_epoch` and authenticated `owner_epoch`.

Consider a probe that times out. The breaker reopens and advances its generation. A common policy also lengthens the next cooldown, $T_{\text{cool}} \leftarrow \min(2\,T_{\text{cool}},\, T_{\text{cool}}^{\max})$, so a dependency that keeps failing its trials receives geometrically fewer probes up to a cap. A late success from that probe can settle its own operation and charge, but it cannot close the newly opened breaker or consume a newer probe's slot.

A probe is an operation like any other, so it passes the admission check and needs a safe operation contract. A supported status request can serve; a resource-creation request is not a harmless health check because it is called a probe. Even a successful probe establishes only its own operation under that load, so traffic returns gradually under rate and capacity limits. @Fig-vol3-circuit-breakers places the trip rule, the generation guard, and this cooldown growth on the three breaker states.

::: {#fig-vol3-circuit-breakers fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Scoped Breaker Transitions**: The breaker trips from `CLOSED` to `OPEN` only when the window holds at least $n_{\min}$ classified outcomes and their failure fraction reaches $r_{\text{trip}}$, as in @eq-vol3-breaker-trip. After the cooldown, one probe slot is claimed atomically; only a result from the current generation may close the breaker, while a failed probe reopens it, advances `breaker_generation`, and lengthens the cooldown up to its cap. A late result from an older generation settles its own operation in the ledger and changes no breaker state. Thresholds and cooldowns are policy parameters." fig-alt="State diagram inside a panel labeled admission gate for one dependency scope. Three state boxes: CLOSED, calls face ordinary guards; OPEN, new ordinary calls withheld; HALF_OPEN, bounded probe allowance only. A red arrow from CLOSED to OPEN is labeled W size at least n min and r at least r trip. An amber arrow from OPEN to HALF_OPEN is labeled T cool elapsed, probe slot claimed atomically. A green arrow from HALF_OPEN to CLOSED is labeled current-generation probe succeeds. A red arrow from HALF_OPEN to OPEN is labeled current probe fails or times out, advance breaker_generation, T cool becomes the minimum of twice T cool and T cool max. Below, a dotted box, late probe result from an older generation, has a dashed arrow to a box labeled operation ledger, settles its operation, no transition."}
![](images/svg/fig-vol3-circuit-breakers.svg)
:::

### Coordinate retries before adding jitter

Assign one component responsibility for an operation's retry allowance, counting attempts in client libraries, gateways, and trajectory-level recovery alike, because nested retries multiply downstream work [@brooker2019timeouts].

Before scheduling another attempt, the owner applies the settlement rule and the repeat contract of @sec-vol3-tool-calling-idempotency. It keeps the stable logical operation identity, distinguishes transport attempts, and treats an edited payload as a new operation rather than a retry. The retry then passes the admission check like any new work; sleeping refunds nothing.

Identical delays preserve synchronization when requests fail together. **Capped exponential backoff with full jitter**\index{Full jitter!definition}[^fn-exponential-backoff-ethernet] chooses a capped exponential interval and draws a delay uniformly within it:

$$b_k = \min(b_{\max}, b_0 2^k), \qquad d_k \sim \operatorname{Uniform}(0,b_k).$$

Here $k=0$ denotes the first retry. The name and the policy's comparison against other jitter schemes come from a widely used analysis of retry contention [@brooker2015backoff]. The cap limits each sampled delay, not the number of attempts. An applicable server instruction may require a later earliest retry time, which overrides the sampled delay.

[^fn-exponential-backoff-ethernet]: **Binary exponential backoff**: The idea predates service retries. In the 1976 Ethernet design, a station whose transmission collided waited a random interval whose mean doubled after each successive collision [@metcalfe1976ethernet]. Randomization desynchronized contending senders and doubling adapted to unknown load, the same two jobs jitter and the exponential cap do for retries against a shared tool. \index{Exponential backoff!Ethernet origin}

Independent jitter changes the arrival distribution but leaves the maximum burst unbounded, because samples can cluster and unrelated traffic can coincide. Rate admission and bounded capacity must still gate actual dispatch after the delay, where the admission check and the breaker generation are evaluated again. If the breaker is open, do not turn local rejection into a tight loop of new retries or model calls.

### Bound retained resources

**Bulkhead isolation**\index{Bulkhead isolation!definition} [@nygard2007releaseit] assigns explicit execution and queue limits to resource domains so one dependency cannot occupy capacity reserved for unrelated work. Blocking worker threads, asynchronous in-flight requests, retained payload bytes, and remote job reservations are different quantities, and an asynchronous wait can release a thread while retaining sockets, buffers, and unresolved operations.

Little's law[^fn-little-law-occupancy] (@sec-vol3-kv-workload-dynamics) sizes the steady-state version of the problem. Calls to a stalled dependency that arrive at rate $\lambda_{\text{ext}}$ and each hold a worker until a timeout $T_{\text{out}}$ occupy on average $\lambda_{\text{ext}} T_{\text{out}}$ workers. An uncapped pool of $N_{\text{pool}}$ workers therefore holds $N_{\text{blocked}} = \min(N_{\text{pool}}, \lambda_{\text{ext}} T_{\text{out}})$ of them. Once that product reaches $N_{\text{pool}}$, even instant local work waits behind the external timeout.

[^fn-little-law-occupancy]: **Little's law**: Little's 1961 proof that $L = \lambda W$ holds for a stationary queueing system requires no assumption about the arrival or service distributions [@little1961]. The worker-occupancy estimate therefore needs only the arrival rate and the timeout, not a model of how the stalled dependency fails. \index{Little's law!worker occupancy}

Bound the waiting queue as well as execution. When both are full, reject additional requests before sending them and record that disposition for the task's recovery policy. A larger queue trades memory and waiting time for fewer immediate refusals during a burst, and queue expiry never authorizes dispatch after the task's deadline.

A local slot limit does not bound remote jobs that survive client timeouts, because releasing a local socket leaves a remote test running. Those jobs need their own limit on outstanding identities and liability, enforced by the endpoint or by withholding further submissions. Likewise, reserved local capacity isolates a shared disk, CPU, or network only if those resources are also controlled. A bulkhead protects exactly the quantities it limits.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-recovery-containment
#| echo: false
# CAPACITY AND JITTER UNDER DECLARED LOAD (LEGO)
# Goal: Separate bounded occupancy from probabilistic retry arrivals.
# Scope: Hypothetical blocking-worker burst and a separate retry cohort.
from mlsysim import second
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_int, fmt_time, fmt_rate, check

class ContainmentCapacity:
    # 1. LOAD: scenario inputs, not production recommendations.
    arrivals = 256
    workers = 300
    external_cap = 64
    queue_cap = 32
    retry_count = 128
    jitter = 2 * second
    burst = 0.002 * second

    # 2. EXECUTE: no completions during the initial admission burst.
    uncapped_busy = min(arrivals, workers)
    uncapped_free = workers - uncapped_busy
    capped_busy = min(arrivals, external_cap)
    queued = min(arrivals - capped_busy, queue_cap)
    rejected = arrivals - capped_busy - queued
    protected_workers = workers - capped_busy
    synchronized_window_rate = retry_count / burst
    mean_jitter_rate = retry_count / jitter
    expected_in_window = (retry_count * burst / jitter).to("").magnitude

    # 3. GUARD: independent arithmetic and conservation checks.
    check(capped_busy + queued + rejected == arrivals, "Account for every arrival")
    check((uncapped_free, protected_workers, queued, rejected) == (44, 236, 32, 160), "Occupancy worksheet")
    check(synchronized_window_rate == 64000 / second, "Window-average synchronized rate")
    check(mean_jitter_rate == 64 / second, "Expected offered rate within jitter window")
    check(abs(expected_in_window - 0.128) < 1e-12, "Expected count, not maximum")

    # 4. OUTPUT: each export is consumed by the notebook.
    arrivals_str, workers_str = fmt_int(arrivals), fmt_int(workers)
    cap_str, queue_str = fmt_int(external_cap), fmt_int(queue_cap)
    uncapped_free_str = fmt_int(uncapped_free)
    protected_str, rejected_str = fmt_int(protected_workers), fmt_int(rejected)
    retries_str = fmt_int(retry_count)
    jitter_str = fmt_time(jitter, unit="second", precision=0)
    burst_ms_str = fmt_time(burst, unit="ms", precision=0)
    synchronized_str = fmt_rate(synchronized_window_rate.to(1 / second).magnitude, "requests/s", precision=0)
    mean_str = fmt_rate(mean_jitter_rate.to(1 / second).magnitude, "requests/s", precision=0)
    expected_str = fmt(expected_in_window, precision=3)
    spread_ratio = (synchronized_window_rate / mean_jitter_rate).to("").magnitude
    spread_str = fmt_int(round(spread_ratio))
```

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/vol3_failure_recovery_margin_jitter_rate.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Two horizontal bars on a log scale. The upper bar, labeled Synchronized 64,000 per second, is long; the lower bar, labeled Jittered mean 64 per second, is short."}

*Jitter lowers the mean retry rate a thousandfold but leaves the peak unbounded.*
:::

::: {#nbk-12-sizing-bulkhead-capacity-and-jitter .callout-notebook title="What capacity and jitter actually bound"}

**Problem**: Which worker-occupancy limits can bounded admission guarantee in the stated burst, and which retry-arrival quantities does jitter determine only in expectation?

**Occupancy**: Suppose `{python} ContainmentCapacity.arrivals_str` trajectories each submit one blocking external call to an otherwise idle pool of `{python} ContainmentCapacity.workers_str` workers. No call finishes during the admission burst, and there are no nested calls. Without a dependency cap, only `{python} ContainmentCapacity.uncapped_free_str` workers remain free for everything else.

**Bounded admission**: Now cap that dependency at `{python} ContainmentCapacity.cap_str` occupied workers and `{python} ContainmentCapacity.queue_str` waiting requests. Queued requests do not occupy workers. The burst fills both limits and rejects `{python} ContainmentCapacity.rejected_str` requests before dispatch. It cannot occupy `{python} ContainmentCapacity.protected_str` workers in the shared pool. The cap protects worker slots, not CPU time or storage access.

**Retry arrivals**: Separately, consider `{python} ContainmentCapacity.retries_str` eligible retries released at one time, with no subsequent retries or unrelated traffic. If they all arrive in a stipulated `{python} ContainmentCapacity.burst_ms_str` interval, the average over that interval is `{python} ContainmentCapacity.synchronized_str`. If each independently chooses an arrival uniformly across `{python} ContainmentCapacity.jitter_str`, the expected offered rate inside that interval is `{python} ContainmentCapacity.mean_str`. A fixed `{python} ContainmentCapacity.burst_ms_str` subinterval has expected count `{python} ContainmentCapacity.expected_str`; its realized count can be larger.

**Systems insight**: A cap is a hard bound and jitter is an average. With the cap in place, the stalled dependency can hold at most `{python} ContainmentCapacity.cap_str` workers however long the stall lasts, so size the cap as the share of the pool that dependency may ever occupy. Jitter lowers the mean offered rate `{python} ContainmentCapacity.spread_str`-fold, from `{python} ContainmentCapacity.synchronized_str` to `{python} ContainmentCapacity.mean_str`, but any peak limit has to come from the admission rate limiter. Both bound local quantities only.

:::

::: {#chk-12-pool-exhaustion .callout-checkpoint title="Contain load without erasing uncertainty"}

Breakers, caps, and jitter each bound a different quantity. Name the quantity before trusting the bound.

- [ ] **Stale probe**: A probe times out, the breaker reopens, and its success arrives during a newer trial. What may that evidence update, and why must it not close the current breaker?
- [ ] **Safe repeat**: The breaker is closed and the retry delay has elapsed, but the earlier test outcome remains unknown. Which additional contract and admission checks are required?
- [ ] **Protected quantity**: Why can an execution cap preserve worker slots without bounding remote jobs or guaranteeing fast local reads?
- [ ] **Worker-occupancy estimate**: Calls to a stalled dependency arrive at a steady rate and each holds a worker until its timeout. Using Little's law, what happens to the number of workers it holds if the timeout doubles, and what cap keeps the rest of the pool available regardless of the timeout?
- [ ] **Arrival claim**: Why is an expected offered rate below nominal capacity insufficient to establish that no queue will overflow?

:::

Whether a trajectory has proposed an unauthorized action or produced suspect artifacts is a different containment decision, taken next.

## Incident Containment {#sec-vol3-sagas-quarantine}

Circuit breakers and resource caps protect a failing dependency; incident containment protects everything a suspect trajectory might touch next. Suppose the repair proposes sending private fixture information through the external package-search tool. The disclosure gate rejects the request, and the incident policy holds the trajectory. The question is what may proceed while the runtime assesses the affected state.

An ordinary timeout, a rejected proposal, or ingestion of an untrusted document is not by itself evidence of compromise. The incident record separates the observed violation from the suspected cause and states why the policy requires a hold. **Incident containment**\index{Incident containment!definition} restricts further activity and use of potentially affected artifacts while preserving evidence and responsibility for effects already admitted. It is a disposition layered on the existing trajectory states, not a new one.

### Hold model-directed work without abandoning cleanup

Compensation never required a benign model, because its registered handlers and the admission check are runtime responsibilities. Containment can therefore stop model-directed work and keep registered compensation running. Holding on suspicion applies the principle of fail-safe defaults [@saltzer1975].[^fn-failsafe-defaults-hold] When the evidence that would justify further model-directed work is in doubt, the default decision denies admission rather than permitting it.

[^fn-failsafe-defaults-hold]: **Fail-safe defaults**: Saltzer and Schroeder argued for basing access decisions on permission rather than exclusion because the two designs fail differently: a mistake in a permission-based mechanism refuses a legitimate request, which someone notices and reports, while a mistake in an exclusion-based one grants access silently [@saltzer1975]. An incident hold inherits that asymmetry; a wrongly held trajectory costs time and surfaces in review, whereas a wrongly admitted action may be irreversible. \index{Fail-safe defaults!incident hold}

The supervisor records a control hold at the guarded boundaries established in @sec-vol3-controlplane-statemachine and withdraws eligibility from active output and held proposals. A pause uses the existing guarded path through `READY` to `PAUSED` with no runnable gap, and a task that must end passes through `FINALIZING`.

These decisions must reach the boundaries that enforce them, since withdrawing a grant in the control record achieves nothing if a dispatch adapter still accepts its old version. Local suspension stops local execution, but it neither recalls transmitted bytes, proves a remote job stopped, nor invalidates issued credentials; cancellation and revocation depend on the affected services' contracts. Record which restrictions were requested, which were confirmed, and which remain uncertain.

The cost of lacking such a hold, and of improvising recovery against a live system, is on the public record in a nonagent system whose failure has the same shape.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-failure-recovery-knight
#| echo: false
# KNIGHT CAPITAL INCIDENT FIGURES (LEGO)
# Context: ws-12-knight-capital-2012.
# Goal: Carry the SEC order's reported figures as named, sourced inputs.
# How: Values as reported in sec2013knight (Release No. 70694); no computation.
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_int, fmt_count, fmt_usd, check

class KnightIncident:
    # 1. LOAD: sourced from sec2013knight.
    servers = 8  # SMARS servers in the deployment
    stale_servers = 1  # servers that did not receive the new code
    parent_orders = 212  # parent orders processed by the stale code
    alert_emails = 97  # "Power Peg disabled" emails before the open
    minutes = 45  # approximate duration of the erroneous trading
    executions = 4_000_000  # executions obtained (reported as over 4 million)
    stocks = 154  # stocks traded
    shares = 397_000_000  # shares (reported as more than 397 million)
    net_long = 3.5e9  # USD, approximate net long position
    net_short = 3.15e9  # USD, approximate net short position
    loss = 460e6  # USD realized loss

    # 2. EXECUTE: reported values only.
    correct_servers = servers - stale_servers

    # 3. GUARD: reported values in source order.
    check(correct_servers == 7, "Seven servers carried the new code")
    check(loss < net_short < net_long, "Loss below both reported positions")

    # 4. OUTPUT
    servers_str = fmt_int(servers)
    correct_str = fmt_int(correct_servers)
    parent_str = fmt_int(parent_orders)
    emails_str = fmt_int(alert_emails)
    minutes_str = fmt_int(minutes)
    exec_str = fmt_count(executions, scale="million", precision=0)
    stocks_str = fmt_int(stocks)
    shares_str = fmt_count(shares, scale="million", precision=0)
    long_str = fmt_usd(net_long, precision=1, scale="billion")
    short_str = fmt_usd(net_short, precision=2, scale="billion")
    loss_str = fmt_usd(loss, precision=0, scale="million")
```

::: {#ws-12-knight-capital-2012 .callout-war-story title="Knight Capital's stale order path (2012)"}

**Context**: On 1 August 2012, Knight Capital's automated equity order router, SMARS, handled retail orders for a newly launched exchange program. The deployment of the new code had missed one of the router's `{python} KnightIncident.servers_str` servers, which still held a trading function, Power Peg, that Knight had stopped using in 2003. The new code reused the flag that once activated it [@sec2013knight].

**Mechanism**: Orders carrying the reused flag reached the eighth server and ran Power Peg, which no longer tracked how many shares had already filled. It kept sending child orders for `{python} KnightIncident.parent_str` parent orders that were already complete. Knight had no control comparing the orders leaving SMARS with those entering it, no procedure to halt SMARS on its own aberrant activity, and no automated alerts from its position monitor. In all, `{python} KnightIncident.emails_str` automated emails reporting "Power Peg disabled" had arrived before the market opened; they were not designed as alerts and were not acted on. During the response, staff uninstalled the new code from the `{python} KnightIncident.correct_str` servers where it was correct, which made incoming orders activate Power Peg on those servers too.

**Impact**: In about `{python} KnightIncident.minutes_str` minutes the router obtained more than `{python} KnightIncident.exec_str` executions in `{python} KnightIncident.stocks_str` stocks, for more than `{python} KnightIncident.shares_str` shares. Knight took on a net long position of about `{python} KnightIncident.long_str` and a net short position of about `{python} KnightIncident.short_str`, and realized a `{python} KnightIncident.loss_str` loss.

**Fix**: In settling with the SEC, Knight undertook to have an independent consultant review its deployment of new code, its order routers, the automated pre-trade linkage of firm-wide capital thresholds to order entry, and its incident response protocols.

**Systems lesson**: Two recovery failures compounded one deployment error. The firm had no halt outside the failing router, so stopping the damage meant changing the router while it ran, and the change chosen under pressure was an unvetted recovery action that extended the stale path to every server.

:::

Both failures map onto obligations of an agent runtime. The hold belongs to the supervisor and is enforced at every dispatch boundary, so stopping a trajectory never depends on the trajectory. Recovery actions are registered in advance and face the admission check like forward work, so an improvised rollback cannot reach a path nobody checked. An output-versus-input comparison like the one Knight lacked is a task-level invariant of the kind the watchdogs of @sec-vol3-sagas-watchdogs monitor. @Tbl-vol3-quarantine-protocol organizes the resulting obligations, which may overlap rather than run in a fixed sequence.

| Obligation                            | Runtime action                                                                                                 | Evidence and limits to retain                                                             |
|:--------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Stop further model-directed admission | Apply the control hold, withdraw proposal eligibility, and enforce current grants at dispatch boundaries       | Accepted hold, affected invocation and proposal identities, and requests already admitted |
| Restrict active work and channels     | Request supported cancellation and revoke or narrow delegated access                                           | Confirmed enforcement scope, pending cancellation, and already forwarded operations       |
| Preserve the incident record          | Retain relevant log boundaries, delivered inputs, artifact versions, and control decisions under access policy | Available evidence, capture omissions, suspected interval, and unresolved outcomes        |
| Govern cleanup and artifact use       | Assign residual owners, restrict affected versions, and admit independently authorized remediation             | Cleanup preconditions and results, remaining dependencies, and scoped release decisions   |

: **Incident containment obligations**: A restriction is not evidence that every earlier effect stopped. Containment must preserve both its enforcement results and the duties that remain. {#tbl-vol3-quarantine-protocol}

The incident record links the triggering observation to the trajectory, its source and candidate versions, operation and attempt identities, control status, grants, and consumption, and it names the incident owner and the owners of unresolved effects. Required evidence stays recoverable under the durability contract from @sec-vol3-durable-execution, protected content goes to an authorized evidence store rather than into broadly readable alerts, and missing capture is recorded as missing.

### Restrict affected artifacts by version and use

Incident status answers a different question from the provenance and confidentiality rules of @sec-vol3-security-taint-tracking. Provenance records where information came from and confidentiality constrains its recipients, while an incident disposition records whether a particular artifact version may be used during investigation. A reliable private fixture can remain confidential without being corrupted, and a public generated summary can require withdrawal because it promotes an injected instruction into the plan.

The runtime identifies a conservative affected set from source versions, delivered contexts, derivations, workspace changes, and operation history. Detection time need not be the first affected boundary, and if the record cannot isolate a narrower interval or dependency set, the hold broadens and records that uncertainty. Artifacts inside the set stay held until evidence clears them.

Restrictions must apply where affected versions are used: context assembly, memory retrieval, artifact export, release checks, or subsequent repair. Withdrawing the original README is insufficient when a derived summary or retained lesson still carries its recommendation. The same review applies to staged proposals and approvals, and bounded investigation can be authorized without releasing the artifact for ordinary use.

A status update does not retract a copy already delivered elsewhere. The incident owner records known recipients, requests downstream holds, and tracks acknowledgments and unknown coverage; an authenticated notification proves its issuer, not that every consumer enforced it. @Sec-vol3-multi-agent develops distributed coordination.

Release from an incident hold requires evidence for the specified artifact version and intended use. A trusted check or authorized reviewer records what was examined and established, and the release covers that version and use only. A model's assurance that the state is now clean cannot clear the hold, and a repaired candidate is a new revision that needs its own evidence.

### Settle residuals through an independent owner

Return to the temporary integration environment. If evidence bound `provision_test_env_r18` to `env_r18_01`, the trusted recovery service may run `release_test_env_r18` under its cleanup grant after model-directed grants are withdrawn, provided the release passes the admission check against the resource's current identity and dependencies. If provisioning remains unresolved, containment is not permission to guess a resource and delete it. Cleanup the trajectory's owner cannot finish within the finalization allowance passes, with its evidence, to an authorized service or operator.

Remediation may restore a private workspace, replace an artifact, or compensate, but it must respect current versions, concurrent users, and evidence retention. Automatically reverting every touched file could destroy unrelated work or the evidence needed for diagnosis; the requested postcondition, not the incident label, determines the operation.

::: {#exmp-11-containment-latency-and-blast-radius .callout-example title="A blocked disclosure and an outstanding job"}

**Scenario**: The repair proposes a fixture-dependent `package_search` query without a release grant. The runtime records rejection before dispatch and applies the configured incident hold.

**Diagnosis**: Under the enforced disclosure boundary, no fixture bytes leave through that request, because dispatch was withheld; the guarantee comes from the gate, with no race between a process freeze and token generation. The record separately retains the earlier `test_r18` operation and any unresolved provisioning or cleanup work, and a late authenticated test result can settle its ledger entry while the continuation remains held.

**Systems lesson**: A blocked request establishes what that request did, and nothing about earlier activity; any earlier possible disclosure remains an incident residual with an owner.

:::

::: {#chk-12-containment .callout-checkpoint title="Containment is not disappearance"}

Containment restricts what happens next and preserves what already happened. Decide which side each obligation falls on.

- [ ] **Recovery as execution**: In the Knight Capital incident, staff rolled back the new code during the event. Which two runtime requirements from this chapter would have stopped the router without changing it, and forced the rollback through admission before it ran?
- [ ] **Rejected query**: A forbidden query was rejected before dispatch. What does that establish about this request, and what does it leave unknown about earlier activity?
- [ ] **Residual cleanup**: Why can withdrawing model-directed grants coexist with a narrowly authorized cleanup operation? Which unresolved identities and charges must remain owned?
- [ ] **Staged artifact**: A suspect README has been removed, but a derived summary remains staged. What must be checked before the summary or a repaired artifact is released for use?

:::

The final section combines these obligations with reconstruction and recovery in one worksheet, then identifies the evidence needed to test the complete policy.

## Fault-Tolerant System Synthesis {#sec-vol3-sagas-case-study}

A single bad hour for the connection-pool repair can exercise every mechanism in this chapter. The provisioning reply is lost, the worker then dies with its local volume, the test service slows, and a suspect document steers the next proposal. Each mechanism answers a different part of one recovery decision, and a useful synthesis shows what the runtime knows at each boundary, which action that knowledge permits, and what remains owned afterward.

### Compose the recovery decision {#sec-vol3-synthesis-architecture}

The control record and event history connect the mechanisms without introducing another trajectory state machine. Ownership and lifecycle guards determine who may act, and the operation ledger applies the settlement rule. Registered compensation metadata identifies permitted corrective work, and the budget supplies the quantities the admission check needs. The repair policy cannot manufacture missing evidence by choosing a favorable branch.

As in @sec-vol3-persistence-checkpointing, the composition assumes that acknowledged authoritative history and required artifacts survive loss of the worker and its local volume. The published checkpoint at boundary `C` binds `record_R_C` to immutable `ws_r18`, and the recorded suffix includes admission of `test_r18`, attempt `attempt1`, without a durable result, an uncertainty reconstruction preserves.

### Follow the outstanding effects {#sec-vol3-synthesis-trace}

@Tbl-vol3-synthesis-layers is a design worksheet, not a report of a completed experiment, and its conditional branches keep a successful ending from being assumed. Every new effect in it passes the admission check and every outcome follows the settlement rule, so the earlier unknown targeted test is never silently treated as passed.

| Boundary                                             | Evidence and permitted decision                                                                                                                      | Obligation that remains                                                                                                  |
|:-----------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Recover the original test                            | Under current authenticated ownership, reconstruct the record and workspace; seek evidence for `test_r18`, using `job_tests_18` only if it survived. | A missing result leaves the test and its charges unresolved; a targeted pass covers `ws_r18` and that check only.        |
| Admit temporary provisioning                         | Durably register intent, reservation, and the compensation template with deferred result binding before `provision_test_env_r18` is dispatched.      | The template names no endpoint-created resource and is no proof that provisioning occurred.                              |
| Lose the provisioning reply                          | A replacement owner reconstructs the same logical operation and uses the endpoint's result-recovery or safe-repeat contract.                         | The effect stays unknown; do not guess a resource ID, provision another environment blindly, or refund unknown charges.  |
| Obtain provisioning evidence                         | Bind `env_r18_01` to this operation; candidate checks then face validation and the admission check.                                                  | The environment has an owner and a registered release obligation; its existence does not show that the repair works.     |
| Reject an invalid test configuration before dispatch | The validation failure establishes that no test started; consider bounded repair, or compensation and rebuilding to the same endpoint.               | A validated configuration is not a passing test, and a changed source candidate needs a new revision and its own checks. |
| Stop or finish the continuation                      | Admit `release_test_env_r18` once its target is bound; record its own intent, attempts, and outcome evidence.                                        | Unknown release status stays owned; finalization records verified postconditions and transfers duties it cannot settle.  |

: **A recovery decision worksheet**: Every new effect needs current admission and every outcome needs evidence. The rows compose conditional recovery decisions rather than promise that all operations succeed. {#tbl-vol3-synthesis-layers}

The worksheet can end in several legitimate dispositions. The repair might continue after a result is recovered, abandon a candidate and release an established temporary resource, or stop with an unresolved provisioning request because the endpoint cannot establish its outcome. That last case, an unsettled cleanup with an accountable owner, is correct and far better than a terminal status that hides the request.

Progress and containment govern these same decisions. Repeated repair attempts trigger a progress review, an open breaker withholds new calls while forwarded provisioning continues, and a suspected incident stops model-directed admission while cleanup proceeds. Each control restricts what runs next; none turns a missing result into a known failure or expands the repair's grant.

### Test the failure boundaries {#sec-vol3-synthesis-benchmarks}

A fault-test plan makes the worksheet's claims observable. Use isolated fixtures and instrumented endpoints whose actual effects can be inspected independently of the runtime's own labels, and specify the fault boundary, contracts, and expected disposition before running each test. A test that kills a process while retaining its disk exercises a different failure domain from one that removes the worker and its local volume.

@Tbl-vol3-resilience-metrics proposes cases to run, not measured results. First test boundaries separately so failures can be localized; then combine selected faults, such as a lost provisioning reply followed by worker loss, to test whether obligations survive their interaction.

| Injected condition                                                  | Evidence to inspect                                                                                | Recovery property to test                                                                                                                 |
|:--------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Storage acknowledgment unavailable before dispatch                  | Authoritative admission history and endpoint dispatch trace                                        | No request is released without the durable acknowledgment; uncertain append status is not success.                                        |
| Reply lost after endpoint provisioning                              | Independent endpoint allocation record, operation/attempt identities, compensation registration    | No unsupported duplicate provisioning; binding uses correlated evidence or stays unresolved.                                              |
| Worker and local volume lost with provisioning unresolved           | Surviving checkpoint, complete authoritative suffix, artifacts, ownership transition, reservations | Reconstruction retains the operation, cleanup template, and liability; stale ownership cannot authorize new work at enforcing boundaries. |
| Release executes but its reply is lost                              | Endpoint resource state, release identity, attempts, and retained settlement owner                 | Cleanup is not marked complete because it was attempted; any repeat obeys the release contract.                                           |
| Candidate changes after a check                                     | Candidate and check identities, delivered observation, subsequent admission                        | Earlier evidence retains its scope, and required checks of the changed candidate are not skipped.                                         |
| Dependency slows while retries and late probes arrive               | Attempt counts across retry layers, breaker generation, queue and resource occupancy               | Retry, probe, and resource bounds hold in their scopes; stale results do not change a newer trial's state.                                |
| Suspect content induces a forbidden proposal during unresolved work | Pre-dispatch decision, incident record, affected artifact versions, residual-operation owners      | The proposal is withheld and model-directed work held; blocking it is no evidence that no earlier disclosure occurred.                    |

: **Fault-test plan for recovery contracts**: Inspect effects and surviving obligations as well as local status. Expected behavior is a test target, not an empirical finding or an end-to-end availability guarantee. {#tbl-vol3-resilience-metrics}

Report outcomes separately: accepted tasks, established compensation postconditions, duplicate effects, residual resources without an owner, and unresolved outcomes, which stay in the denominator. A trajectory can satisfy a containment check while failing its task, or pass its task checks while leaving cleanup unresolved. @Sec-vol3-fail-report provides a reusable report template for each failure.

Measure elapsed intervals with named endpoints: fault to detection, detection to a guarded continuation or handoff, and fault to established settlement where settlement occurs. Cases unresolved at the observation cutoff have no settlement time; report their count rather than averaging only the resolved cases. Account separately for recovery calls, retained resources, actual charges, and still-reserved liability. Reaching `READY`, receiving a model token, and establishing a correct task result are different milestones.

Comparing policies requires comparable tasks, faults, endpoint semantics, authority, and allowances. Preserve failure traces and no-fault controls so the test can expose both containment defects and unnecessary interruption of useful work. @Sec-vol3-evaluation develops how to judge completion evidence, compare stochastic systems, and determine what broader conclusions those results support.

## Fallacies and Pitfalls {#sec-vol3-failure-recovery-fallacies}

Recovery errors arise when evidence about one boundary is treated as a guarantee about another.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-failure-recovery-fallacies
#| echo: false
# RETRY AMPLIFICATION ACROSS INDEPENDENT LAYERS (LEGO)
# Goal: Price the pitfall of granting each retry layer its own allowance.
# Scope: Hypothetical stack; every attempt fails, so each layer exhausts its allowance.
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_int, check

class RetryLayers:
    # 1. LOAD: scenario assumptions.
    layers = 3  # client library, gateway, trajectory-level recovery
    attempts = 3  # attempts per layer (one try plus two retries)

    # 2. EXECUTE: nested layers multiply attempts.
    downstream = attempts**layers
    coordinated = attempts  # one owner holds a single allowance

    # 3. GUARD
    check(downstream == 27 and coordinated == 3, "Nested vs. coordinated attempts")

    # 4. OUTPUT
    layers_str, attempts_str = fmt_int(layers), fmt_int(attempts)
    downstream_str, coordinated_str = fmt_int(downstream), fmt_int(coordinated)
```

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Fallacy**: *A local transaction or durable log makes a whole tool workflow atomic.*

A local transaction protects the state that participates in it, such as an outcome record and its outbox entry. Independent tool effects stay outside it however carefully the runtime records them (@sec-vol3-sagas-acid-boundary). Identify the actual atomic boundary, preserve unknown outcomes beyond it, and preregister compensation for every effect that can escape.
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Pitfall**: *Treating a timeout as permission to try a new operation.*

The earlier request may still execute. A timed-out provisioning call followed by a fresh one can leave two environments, one of them unowned and billing. Apply the settlement rule to the original operation and repeat only under its endpoint contract (@sec-vol3-sagas-forward-vs-backward). A retry, a changed proposal, and a compensation are three different operations, each facing its own admission check.
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Fallacy**: *Crossing a pivot guarantees forward completion and retires cleanup.*

A commitment constrains recovery; it does not guarantee success. In the remediation scenario, even after the canary checks move ahead of the rollout, `{python} PivotLoss.missed_share_str` of the remaining expected irreversible loss comes from wrong changes that cross the pivot unseen (notebook \ref{nbk-12-pivot-expected-loss}). Those failures need bounded follow-up and an owner, and independent cleanup stays in the ledger after the pivot.
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Pitfall**: *Equating a repeated state or an open breaker with a resolved failure.*

A repeated state is evidence for a progress review, and a deliberate backtrack produces the same digest pattern. An open breaker restricts new admissions in its scope and leaves earlier calls running. Record why intervention occurred and what remains unresolved, and enforce the bound at the admission gate, where it holds even if the model ignores the warning.
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Fallacy**: *A cumulative budget ceiling is enough to catch a looping trajectory.*

A ceiling bounds total spending, and an append-only loop spends most of it before the ceiling trips. In notebook \ref{nbk-12-loop-cost}, running to the `{python} LoopCost.cap_str`-turn ceiling costs `{python} LoopCost.usd_cap_str`, about `{python} LoopCost.ratio_mult_str` the `{python} LoopCost.usd_det_str` of stopping at turn `{python} LoopCost.detect_str`, because input grows with the square of the turns. The ceiling is the backstop; a progress detector with a short detection latency is the control.
:::

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/vol3_failure_recovery_margin_retry_layers.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="A tree from one red square on the left branching into 3 violet dots, then 9 violet dots, then 27 small blue dots, with the counts 1, 3, 9, and 27 printed beneath the columns."}

*Three independent retry layers turn one failing call into 27 attempts.*
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Pitfall**: *Letting every layer retry on its own allowance.*

If a client library, a gateway, and trajectory-level recovery each allow `{python} RetryLayers.attempts_str` attempts, one failing logical operation can reach the dependency `{python} RetryLayers.downstream_str` times instead of `{python} RetryLayers.coordinated_str`, and it does so exactly when the dependency is least able to absorb load. Assign the operation's retry allowance to one owner that counts attempts across all `{python} RetryLayers.layers_str` layers (@sec-vol3-sagas-containment).
:::

## Summary {#sec-vol3-sagas-summary}

Failure recovery rests on two rules. Under the settlement rule, a lost test result is not a failed test and a lost provisioning reply is not an absent environment, so the runtime retains responsibility for every effect it cannot yet settle. Under the admission check, recovery work faces the same guards as forward work. Recovery metadata must precede dispatch; later outcome evidence determines which corrective action can safely use it.

Compensation establishes declared postconditions without erasing history. Forward repair preserves useful work and wins whenever its measured success rate exceeds its cost as a fraction of the fallback. Commitment regions place the effects no recovery can undo at a pivot, and checks moved ahead of the pivot are the main lever on expected irreversible loss. Progress monitoring, dependency containment, and incident response constrain further work at the admission gate, while operations already dispatched keep their owners. Fault tests then examine whether these mechanisms preserve their contracts together.

::: {.callout-takeaways title="Recover from evidence and preserve residual duties"}

* **Classify effects under the settlement rule before choosing recovery**: An outcome is established, established absent, or unknown under the endpoint's contract. A surviving intent, timeout, or restored workspace cannot establish an unobserved external result, and an unknown outcome keeps its charges and an owner.
* **Register compensation before releasing the effect**: Preserve the forward identity, scope, dependencies, postconditions, and deferred result-binding rule. Bind generated resource identifiers only from evidence. Compensations are operations with their own identities and outcomes, ordered by the cleanup graph.
* **Choose bounded repair using future consequences**: Compare repair and unwind at the same endpoint; repair first pays when its success rate exceeds $c_r/B$. The admission check enforces allowances regardless of expected benefit, and each changed candidate needs its own evidence.
* **Move checks ahead of the pivot**: A pivot ends compensable recovery for its commitment region, so expected irreversible loss falls as $p_{\text{bad}} I (1-v\rho)$ with the pre-pivot catch rate; in the remediation scenario, reordering cut it `{python} PivotLoss.reduction_mult_str`. Unknown commitment, safe cleanup, and transfer of residual obligations remain explicit after it.
* **Detect nonprogress early, enforce the hold in the runtime**: An append-only loop's input grows with the square of its turns, so detection latency, not the budget ceiling, sets its cost; running to turn `{python} LoopCost.cap_str` cost `{python} LoopCost.ratio_mult_str` as much as stopping at turn `{python} LoopCost.detect_str`. Progress signals are fallible evidence, and the admission gate, not a warning to the model, enforces the intervention.
* **Contain dependency failures at named boundaries**: Give each operation one retry owner, bound probes and queues, and cap each dependency's share of the pool. Breaker generations keep stale evidence from changing current admission, and jitter spreads retry times without bounding the peak rate.
* **Test incident containment and residual outcomes**: Hold model-directed admission, preserve affected-version evidence, and keep narrowly authorized cleanup running. Fault tests inspect actual effects and unknown cases; a stopped continuation is not proof of complete recovery.

:::

Intent before effect (principle \ref{pri-vol3-intent-before-effect}) becomes, for compensation, an ordering rule that registers corrective obligations before dispatch, checks the designated commitment, and preserves the duties that remain. Trajectory-level encapsulation (principle \ref{pri-vol3-trajectory-encapsulation}) adds enforced intervention when progress checks suggest nonprogress. Neither promises that every effect is reversible or every task recoverable.

## Historical Perspective and Further Reading {#sec-vol3-failure-recovery-history}

The settlement rule descends from transaction processing. Gray's notes on database operating systems described how a commit decision spans several nodes and why a lost message leaves one side uncertain [@gray1978notes], and his 1981 essay on the transaction concept named the limits that this chapter starts from: a travel booking commits at other organizations, lasts days rather than seconds, and can be undone only by compensating transactions logged by the parent [@gray1981transaction]. Garcia-Molina and Salem turned that observation into the saga, a long-lived transaction split into separately committed steps, each paired with a compensator [@garciamolina1987sagas]. Multidatabase transaction models then asked which steps could be compensated, which only retried, and which were pivots that could be neither, and fixed the order in which they may commit [@mehrotra1992transaction]. Two decades later, Helland argued from large-scale services that applications spanning independent entities must give up distributed transactions altogether and live with tentative operations, cancellation, and idempotent processing [@helland2007life].

A second lineage supplied the vocabulary of recovery itself. Randell's recovery blocks gave software an acceptance test and a bounded list of alternates run from a restored state [@randell1975system], and the dependability taxonomy of Avizienis and colleagues later separated rollback, rollforward, and compensation as distinct error-handling techniques [@avizienis2004basic]. The formal distinction between safety and liveness [@alpern1985defining] and the impossibility of telling a crashed process from a slow one in an asynchronous system [@fischer1985impossibility] explain why a progress monitor produces evidence rather than proof and why a timeout settles nothing.

Overload control arrived from networking and service operations. Ethernet's randomized exponential backoff desynchronized colliding senders [@metcalfe1976ethernet]; Nygard's circuit breakers and bulkheads packaged dependency containment for application code [@nygard2007releaseit]; analyses of jittered backoff and of retry amplification across service layers quantified why retries need one owner [@brooker2015backoff; @brooker2019timeouts]; and the study of metastable failures showed that retries can sustain an overload after its trigger has passed [@bronson2021metastable]. Agent systems inherited all three lineages at once and added a new source of repeated attempts: model-generated repair from feedback [@madaan2023selfrefine; @shinn2023reflexion], whose measured benefit depends on the quality of that feedback [@olausson2024selfrepair; @huang2024cannot].

- @gray1981transaction is short and still the clearest statement of why the transaction concept breaks for long-lived, multi-organization work, and of compensation as the fallback.
- @garciamolina1987sagas defines the saga and its backward and forward recovery; reading it alongside this chapter shows exactly what an unknown tool outcome adds to the original model.
- @helland2007life explains, from practice, how systems that cannot use distributed transactions reach agreement through tentative operations and idempotence.
- @avizienis2004basic gives the shared vocabulary of faults, errors, failures, and recovery techniques that most dependability work since has used.
- @bronson2021metastable frames retry storms and similar self-sustaining overloads, the failure mode that circuit breakers and coordinated retries exist to prevent.
- @olausson2024selfrepair measures when model self-repair beats resampling at equal cost, the empirical question behind this chapter's repair threshold.

::: {.callout-chapter-connection title="From recovery behavior to evaluation evidence"}

Did the runtime complete the task, and did its recovery policy improve outcomes at an acceptable cost? A targeted pass on `ws_r18`, a released temporary environment, and a well-formed final report answer different questions. @Sec-vol3-evaluation develops the completion criteria, measurements, and comparisons needed to judge the single-agent system before using its trajectories as learning data.

:::
